item.title: Cancer Can Be Emotionally as Well as Physically Devastating
item.description:
Depression

Cancer Can Be Emotionally as Well as Physically Devastating

When cancer causes depression, what can help both?

Posted July 31, 2026

Key points
  • Cancer impacts emotional as well as physical health.
  • Emotional distress, and especially depression, can dampen the effectiveness of physical interventions.
  • Getting information on emotional treatment options, therefore, is vital for successful cancer treatment.
Facing a serious, painful, and potentially fatal illness?
Source: Adrian Swancar / Unsplash

When Josh first heard his doctor speak the dreaded word “cancer,” his first reaction was disbelief. “How could I have cancer? I’m in my early fifties, in great health, and have a great life!”

Unfortunately, before long, the reality of Josh’s illness struck him.

As Josh saw with increasing clarity the long road ahead of pain, suffering, and inability to enjoy the activities that for so many years had given him both pleasure and a sense of purpose, an intense wave of anxiety swept over him. Like a man standing on the edge of the shore who had been knocked over by an unexpected strong wave, Josh felt himself losing his emotional balance, overcome by dread and fright.

Next came the anger. “Why me?”

And then the strongest wave yet hit Josh, a wave of hopelessness and helplessness. Josh’s wife said to him, “You sound so depressed! That’s not like you!”

Josh agreed. Depression was not an emotional challenge he had faced before, or knew how to deal with now.

Was Josh’s case unique?

Josh’s reaction to his cancer diagnosis is likely to feel all too familiar to anyone who has been faced with this illness.

As Annika Ellis, an advocacy associate from the cancer advocacy organization Mesothelioma Hope, explains, “While cancer discussions often center on physical health and treatment options, it’s equally important to address the mental health needs of patients. A cancer diagnosis can be overwhelming, leading to a range of emotions, such as fear, anxiety, and even depression. This is why mental health support is crucial for enhancing the overall well-being of those battling cancer.”

All too often, Annika went on to explain, “Cancer patients’ emotional needs get ignored by the treating medical professionals. They most likely assume that as the cancer gets treated, the clients will feel better emotionally as well.”

What are negative reciprocal interaction cycles?

While there is definitely some truth to the assumption that curing a cancer will cure the depression triggered by cancer, the opposite also can be true. The presence of cancer can create a negative reciprocal interaction cycle. That is, the illness creates depression, which in turn exacerbates the illness, which in turn makes the illness worse, and so the cycle spins.

Thus, the thoughts and feelings of hopelessness and helplessness generated by depression actually hamper the body’s will and ability to fight off an illness, including cancer.

What has medical research found about the impacts of depression on the effectiveness of cancer treatment?

A landmark 2010 study by Pinquart & Duberstein reviewed 76 prior studies investigating whether depression hindered cancer treatment. The findings were striking. Depression predicted a significantly higher risk that the patient would die, even after controlling for the type and severity of the cancer.

In the subsequent decade and a half, more studies have detailed similar findings.

Most recently, Ungvari et al. (2025/2026) reviewed 65 recent studies. They found that depression increased the rate of patients dying from cancer by between 23 percent and a whopping 83 percent.

The good news

Where, then, can cancer patients and their families find emotional support and treatment? Organizations, like Mesothelioma Hope, where Annika Ellis works, and other online resources can help.

In addition, learn about self-help anti-depression treatments for interventions that do not require adding anti-depressant medication to a body that is already medically vulnerable. I explain several of these techniques in my book Prescriptions Without Pills: For Relief From Depression, Anger, Anxiety, and More, as these interventions may be able to make a massive impact on your body’s ability to fight cancer—and win the battle.

In sum, if you are struggling with cancer, get the information you need to address the emotional challenges that this illness almost inevitably triggers.

Information is power. Get it, and use it!

item.title: Judicial Rejection of “Stop Woke” Laws for Higher Education
item.description:
Education

Judicial Rejection of “Stop Woke” Laws for Higher Education

Implications for mental health education when courts overturn anti-DEI laws.

Posted July 31, 2026

Key points
  • Some states have passed laws restricting educators from teaching particular DEI-related topics.
  • A recent court decision suggests prohibiting certain topics from being taught violates freedom speech.
  • Protecting free speech in professional education is vital to ensuring MHPs are properly prepared for practice.

Since 2023, approximately 18 states have passed laws restricting diversity, equity, and inclusion (DEI) initiatives in higher education (Hoyos Ensuncho, 2025). These measures vary considerably. Some prohibit public universities from having DEI offices, mandatory training, or diversity statements; others regulate curricula or restrict how professors may address concepts involving race, sex, privilege, discrimination, and oppression. The effects of these extend beyond removing certain topics from university curricula. Faculty members have reported changing how they teach, limiting their research, and leaving institutions due to anti-DEI laws (Hoyos Ensuncho, 2025).

For psychology, social work, counseling, and other mental health-related programs, anti-DEI laws raise particular concerns. Professional ethical standards require students to develop the knowledge, skills, values, and attitudes needed to work with clients and communities from diverse backgrounds (ACA, 2014; APA, 2017; Barsky, 2023; NASW, 2021). This includes learning about how to practice effectively with people from different cultures, genders, sexualities, socioeconomic statuses, abilities and disabilities, religions, immigration statuses, and other aspects of human diversity. How can future MHPs develop cultural competence and cultural humility if educators are discouraged or prohibited from examining these subjects with students.

The Pernell Decision

On July 7, 2026, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 11th Circuit addressed that question in Pernell v. Lamb. The court found that certain sections of Florida’s “Stop WOKE Act” were unconstitutional, particularly as they applied to higher education. The court suggested that the state could not selectively prohibit public-university professors from expressing particular viewpoints about race, sex, privilege, and oppression merely because government officials disapprove of them. As the majority noted, “the government cannot forbid what it perceives as heresy” (Pernell, p. 50). Accordingly, the court held that these provisions of the “Stop WOKE Act” violated the free speech provisions of the U.S. Constitution. This decision also aligns with the principles of academic freedom. While the court’s ruling is an appellate decision related specifically to Florida’s anti-DEI law, it could have implications for similar laws passed in other states.

Impact of the Decision for Mental Health Education

The Pernell decision protects the ability of educators at Florida’s public colleges and universities to teach about culturally responsive mental health practice without being required to adopt the state’s preferred positions. Accordingly, mental health educators may prepare students to:

  • examine their own cultural assumptions, worldviews, and biases;
  • understand how culture and social context influence distress, coping, diagnosis, and help-seeking;
  • explore the effects of discrimination, privilege, poverty, migration, trauma, and marginalization;
  • conduct culturally responsive assessments;
  • adapt interventions to clients’ needs and values;
  • discuss race, gender, sexuality, religion, disability, and other social identities when clinically relevant; and
  • use a person-centered approach to clinical practice, treating clients as experts on their own lives, beliefs, relationships, rituals, languages, and worldviews.

Culturally informed education is not simply an ideological preference. It is required for effective practice. A systematic review found that cultural-competence training can improve mental health professionals’ attitudes, knowledge, and skills (Chu et al., 2022). A meta-analysis found that clients’ perceptions of therapists’ cultural humility were strongly associated with the therapeutic alliance and moderately associated with psychotherapy improvement (Orlowski et al., 2025). Another systematic review found that clients’ experiences of clinicians’ cultural awareness, responsiveness, and discriminatory behavior had positive effects on access to care and the quality of clinician-client relationships (Sadusky et al., 2024).

Reasons for Continued Caution

While the Pernell v. Lamb decision is significant, it does not resolve all concerns about DEI and higher education. First, the Eleventh Circuit’s decision is binding on federal courts in Alabama, Florida, and Georgia. Its reasoning may serve as persuasive authority elsewhere, but courts in other federal circuits are not required to follow it.

Second, the court affirmed a preliminary injunction. Although the majority concluded that the challenged provisions were unconstitutional as applied to public postsecondary professors, further litigation on this case remains possible.

Third, other anti-DEI laws use different language and regulate different activities. Some target classroom instruction, while others regulate required courses, employee training, DEI offices, hiring practices, or institutional expenditures. Each law must be evaluated according to its particular wording and legal context.

Finally, the chilling effect may continue even when a law is blocked. Faculty members may still fear complaints, investigations, retribution, or political criticism (Hoyos Ensuncho, 2026). Administrators may respond cautiously, and educators may avoid subjects that students or public officials might find uncomfortable.

Discomfort, however, is not necessarily evidence of harm. Mental health education sometimes requires students to examine challenging questions about bias, inequality, identity, trauma, and professional power. Educators should facilitate these conversations respectfully and without humiliating, stereotyping, or coercing students. Still, avoiding controversial subjects altogether may leave future MHPs poorly prepared for helping clients in a culturally informed manner.

Academic Freedom and Professional Education

The American Association of University Professors (n.d.) defines academic freedom as “the freedom of a teacher or researcher in higher education to investigate and discuss the issues in their academic field, and to teach and publish findings without interference from administrators, boards of trustees, political figures, donors, or other entities.” While academic freedom protects the right of faculty members to speak freely, faculty members in professional education must also ensure that they exercise this right in a manner that prepares mental health students for the demands of clinical practice. Accordingly, faculty members should not only present students with specific research, knowledge, and skills required for diversity-informed practice; they should also engage students in critical reflection and thinking. This process includes examining various sources of theory and research, considering competing perspectives, questioning assumptions, and reaching informed conclusions.

Conclusion

Pernell v. Lamb affirms the principle that while government officials may establish certain types of standards for higher education, they may not prohibit educators from engaging students in particular discussions about diversity, equity, inclusion, or other topics that the current government disfavors. For MHPs, this case is not simply about constitutionally protected free speech and academic inquiry. It is also about ensuring that future professionals can provide ethical, culturally responsive, and person-centered care.

item.title: Don’t Let AI Speak for the Dead
item.description:
Grief

Don’t Let AI Speak for the Dead

What we lose when an app remembers our dead for us.

Posted July 31, 2026

Key points
  • AI “grief bots” trained on the dead person’s data promise to let mourners keep the conversation going.
  • Continuing bonds theory holds that carrying the dead within us is healthy—but the carrying is work.
  • Healing from loss and the business model point in opposite directions.
  • Outsourcing remembrance to an app risks the same fate as outsourcing navigation: the capacity fades.

I think of my mother every day. She’s there when I cook the food she used to cook for me, when I smell the flowers she loved, and when I face a tough decision at work. Her voice arrives unbidden, in moments of both strain and joy, and sometimes it feels like we talk more than we did when she was alive.

Psychologists have a name for this. They call it continuing bonds theory—the idea that a healthy relationship with someone we’ve lost doesn’t end at death. We continue to carry the dead with us after their passing: in memory, in ritual, in the inner dialogue that never quite stops. According to continuing bonds theory, this is a healthy and even necessary part of the grief process.

And now there is an industry that would like to monetize it.

Source: Bluum / Adobe Stock

The “Generative Ghosts”

CBS News recently reported on a growing sector of startups offering “generative ghosts.” These are AI chatbots trained on a dead person’s emails, photos, social media posts, and voice recordings, so that family and friends can keep talking with them after they’re gone.

Your mother’s voice, for $20 a month.

The marketing promises solace and a bridge back to the people and the moments that we miss. I understand the attraction, because I feel the ache.

But the promise deserves scrutiny. Let’s start with the obvious danger.

The Business Model of Grief

The end-point of grief is integration—to find peace with grief while continuing to carry it. But that’s not what the grief-tech subscription wants. For the apps, every month you keep talking to the ghost is revenue; the moment your grief metabolizes into peace, the product has lost its customer. Grief tech inherits the design logic of every other product of the attention economy: optimized for engagement. And the engagement loop now runs through the most defenseless part of you.

The problem is structural—the healing process and the business model point in opposite directions. No founder needs to set out to trap the bereaved. The incentives do the work on their own: features that deepen the bond, notifications in her voice, an anniversary message you didn’t ask for. The product gets better and better at simulating her, which means it gets better and better at being needed.

And there is a second death waiting at the end of it. When the startup folds, or the model changes, or the price goes up—you lose her again, this time on a corporate timetable.

These are real dangers, but there is an even deeper one.

Carrying Her

As I have learned over the last year, the dead speak to us. I ask my mother things all the time, and she answers in her voice, with her certainties, sometimes telling me what I would rather not hear.

And the point is that her voice lives in me. It is built from a lifetime of knowing her, and it is kept alive by the daily work of remembering her.

I have to keep doing this work if I want to keep hearing her.

This, I have come to believe, is both the long labor of grief and simultaneously its deepest privilege: to move the one we love from the world into ourselves, until we become the place where they live.

The generative ghost destroys both the labor (which is why it’s so attractive) and the privilege (which is why it is so dangerous). The grief bots tell us that we don’t have to work at remembering the dead, because the bots will host them for us. And so the dead move out of us and onto servers. We type, the bot answers. The relationship stops being something we sustain and becomes something we access.

In fact, there is no relationship anymore. There is only a transaction.

And we already know how this ends up, because we have run the experiment on ourselves before. When we handed our sense of direction to navigation apps, the capacities we stopped using didn’t wait patiently for our return. Researchers found that the more people relied on GPS, the worse their spatial memory became when they had to navigate on their own—and the heaviest users declined the fastest over time.

So what happens to the memory of my mother when I stop remembering her myself and let an app do it for me?

6 Practices for Carrying

Here are six practices that keep the dead where they belong—in us:

  1. Keep one bounded ritual. Seeing an old picture, eating a special meal, taking a walk they loved. Grief needs its memorials.
  2. Cook their food, and use their phrases. Carrying is a practice, not a mood. Do one thing this week the way they would have done it.
  3. Visit the spaces they used to inhabit. People live in specific places, and so do our memories of them. Spend an hour this week in a place they loved.
  4. Say them aloud. Share a memory with someone who knew them. The dead live most vividly between people.
  5. Let the wave come. When grief arrives, resist the reach for a screen. Sit with it for five minutes before you do anything at all.

From Inside

I won’t pretend the ghost doesn’t tempt me. There are nights when the ache is bad enough that $20 a month sounds like a bargain—when I would give a great deal to hear her say one new sentence.

And then tomorrow comes, and she says one. She arrives unannounced—at the stove, in the middle of a hard decision—and answers me the way she always does now: from inside.

That is the thing the ghost cannot sell me, because I already have it. The dead don’t need a server to speak to us.

They never did. They just need us to keep carrying them.
